title: Structured concurrency in Kotlin
context: What is structured concurrency in Kotlin coroutines, and why is GlobalScope.launch discouraged in a backend service?
answer: Structured concurrency means every coroutine runs inside a scope that owns it: the parent doesn't complete until its children do, cancelling the parent cancels the children, and a child's failure propagates to the parent. That ties coroutines to a lifecycle such as a request or the application, so nothing leaks and errors aren't lost. GlobalScope has no parent and no lifecycle: its coroutines outlive the request, aren't cancelled on shutdown, and their exceptions only reach the default handler. Use coroutineScope { } for work inside a request, and a CoroutineScope owned by a component (with a SupervisorJob and cancelled on shutdown) for background work.

points.title: Coroutines belong to a scope
points.why: Each coroutine has a parent Job, so scopes form a tree tied to a lifecycle.

points.title: Parent waits for children
points.why: A scope doesn't complete until its children finish, so no work is left running unnoticed.

points.title: Cancellation and errors propagate
points.why: Cancelling the parent cancels children; a failing child cancels its parent and siblings.

points.title: GlobalScope escapes all of this
points.why: Its coroutines outlive requests, aren't cancelled on shutdown, and their errors are easily lost.

points.title: What to use instead
points.why: coroutineScope inside a request; an application-owned CoroutineScope with SupervisorJob for background work.
